data.text:
Asian Films submitted to the Oscar's. Nomination Announcement January 22, 2026

Bangladesh: A House Named Shahana (Leesa Gazi)
Gazi becomes the first woman to represent Bangladesh in the international feature category; the country’s 20 previous entries have brought no nominations. Adapting her own 2011 novella as her debut feature, Gazi’s A House Named Shahana follows a fierce, forthright divorcee in a rural town in ’90s Bangladesh, who defies social stigma and the burden of family honour to live on her own terms. The film debuted at Mumbai Film Festival in 2023, winning the Gender Sensitivity award. International sales: TBC

Bhutan: I, the Song (Dechen Roder)
Bhutan has a colourful Oscar history from just four previous entries. After first submission The Cup was not nominated in 2000, it was 21 years before the country entered again, with Pawo Choyning Dorji’s Lunana: A Yak in the Classroom. The film was disqualified as Bhutan had not established an Academy-approved selection committee; they had done so by the following year, when Lunana was resubmitted and made it to nomination stage. In 2024, Dorji’s The Monk and the Gun made the shortlist. I, the Song is Bhutanese director Roder’s second feature; it debuted at Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival in 2024, going on to festivals including New Horizons in Poland. International sales: Diversion

Cambodia: Tenement (Inrasothythep Neth, Sokyou Chea)
This directorial debut uses folk horror to explore the country’s turbulent past as it follows a Cambodian-Japanese artist who returns home after her mother’s death and is haunted by visions. Tenement had its world premiere at Rotterdam 2024 in the Big Screen Competition and is produced by Westec Media Limited and Kongchak Pictures. Cambodia has been nominated once, in 2013 for Rithy Panh’s The Missing Picture. International sales: Reel Suspects

China: Dead To Rights (Shen Ao)
Set during the 1937-38 Nanjing massacre of Chinese civilians by the Japanese army, Shen’s historical drama follows a group of civilians who seek refuge in a photo studio amid the chaos of war, while risking their lives to expose atrocities. The film was number one at the Chinese box office for several weeks following its release in July 2025; and topped the global box office at the start of August with a worldwide gross of over $300m. The world’s second-most-populous country has never won the international feature award, and has just two nominations from 38 previous entries - for Zhang Yimou and Yang Fengliang’s Ju Dou in 1991, and Zhang’s Hero in 2003. International sales: China Film Group Corporation

Hong Kong: The Last Dance (Anselm Chan)
Chan’s third feature is the highest-grossing local film of all time in Hong Kong, making over $20m following its release in November 2024, after a world premiere as the opening film of Hong Kong Asian Film Festival the previous month. Looking at the deathcare industry (services, policy and governance around death), it follows a wedding planner who enters the funeral industry through a partnership with a Taoist priest. It is Hong Kong’s 44th entry to the best international Oscar award, with three previous nominations - for Zhang Yimou’s Raise the Red Lantern in 1992, Chen Kaige’s Farewell My Concubine in 1994 and Derek Tsang’s Better Days in 2021. International sales: Emperor Motion Pictures

India: Homebound (Neeraj Ghaywan)
Executive produced by Martin Scorsese, this Hindi-language drama centres around two childhood friends who attempt to pass the national police exam. The film had its world premiere in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard strand with further festival outings at Toronto and Zurich. Homebound is produced by Dharma Productions. India has been nominated for an Oscar three times and made the shortlist in 2022 with The Last Film Show. International sales: Paradise City Sales

Indonesia: Sore: Wife From The Future (Yandy Laurens)
Sci-fi romance about a man living alone in Croatia who encounters a woman who claims to be his wife from the future. Adapted from Laurens’ 2017 web series of the same name, it stars Dion Wiyoko and Sheila Dara. The feature proved one of the most-watched local titles of the year with 3 million admissions following its release in July. Indonesia has submitted films since 1987 but has yet to secure a nomination in the category International sales: TBC

Japan: Kokuho (Lee Sang-il)
This three-hour epic about a family of kabuki performers premiered in Directors’ Fortnight at Cannes and has proved a massive box office hit locally, earning nearly $80m (¥11.53bn) to become the second-highest-grossing live-action Japanese film of all time. Korean Japanese director Lee adapted Shuichi Yoshida’s novel about a gifted kabuki performer descended from a family of gangsters, set against postwar Japan’s economic boom. Ryo Yoshizawa and Ryusei Yokohama star alongside Ken Watanabe, previously Oscar-nominated for The Last Samurai. Japan received an Oscar nomination in this category in 2024 with Wim Wenders’ Perfect Days and won the Academy Award in 2022 with Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Drive My Car. Yojiro Takita’s Departures won the Oscar for Japan in 2008. International sales: Pyramide International

Kazakhstan: Cadet (Adilkhan Yerzhanov)
The prolific Yerzhanov has directed an average of one feature per year for 15 years. Cadet garnered wide festival play, launching at Tokyo Film Festival in 2024 and going on to the Berlinale Forum strand. The horror follows a single mother who enrols her son into a military academy, where he is bullied for his feminine appearance. Yerzhanov has made two features since Cadet - 2024’s Mavr and 2025’s Kazakh Scary Tales. Despite his output, he has made just one of his country’s 18 previous Oscar entries - Yellow Cat for 2022 - with one nomination from those films, for Sergei Bodrov’s Mongols in 2008. International sales: TBC

Kyrgyzstan: Black Red Yellow (Aktan Arym Kubat)
Produced by the Kyrgyzstan National Film Studio, Black Red Yellow follows a love story between two ordinary villagers. The film won the Golden Goblet for best film at Shanghai International Film Festival in June 2025. Kyrgyzstani director Kubat has previously made films including Beshkempir: The Adopted Son, The Light Thief, Centaur and This Is What I Remember – all of which were his country’s Oscar entries, for the 1999, 2011, 2018 and 2024 awards. This is Kyrgyzstan’s 18th time entering for the international feature Oscar. It is yet to make the nominations or even shortlisting stage, with two titles – Night Accident for 2019 and This Is What I Remember for 2024 – not making the official list of submitted films. International sales: TBC

Mongolia: Silent City Driver (Janchivdorj Sengedorj)
Winner of the grand prix for best film at Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival in 2024, this drama follows a hearse driver struggling to adjust to life outside of prison who takes solace in caring for stray dogs. The film also screened at Far East Film Festival where it picked up the Purple Mulberry prize. Producers are MFIA, Dominion Tech LLC, Nomadia Pictures and Ddish. Silent City Driver marks Mongolia’s 10th submission to the Oscars, with no nominations as of yet. International sales: TBC

Nepal: Anjila (Milan Chams)
Nepali director Chams is a leading light of his country’s industry, having previously made features including 2018 romance Blind Rocks. His 10th feature is a sports drama based on the real life of Anjila Tumbapo Subba, goalkeeper and captain for Nepal’s women’s football team. Nepal has submitted 14 previous Oscar entries, with a nomination for its first entry in 2000, Eric Valli’s Himalaya/Caravan. International sales: TBC

Papua New Guinea: Papa Buka (Bijukumar Damodaran)
Papa Buka marks the first time that Papua New Guinea has entered the international feature film category at the Oscars. Directed by Indian filmmaker Bijukumar Damodaran (Trees Under the Sun), it follows aging war veteran Papa Buka as he guides two Indian historians uncovering untold Second World War stories connecting India and Papua New Guinea. International sales: TBC

Philippines: Magellan (Lav Diaz)
Gael Garcia Bernal stars as 16th-century Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan, who voyaged to the Malayan Archipelago and became obsessed with conquest and conversion, sparking violent uprisings. The film premiered at Cannes and went on to be selected for Toronto and Busan. Diaz is a prolific Filipino filmmaker who won Locarno’s Golden Leopard in 2014 with From What Is Before, a Berlinale Silver Bear in 2016 with A Lullaby To The Sorrowful Mystery and Venice’s Golden Lion the same year with The Woman Who Left. The Philippines previously submitted Diaz’s work to the Oscars with 2013’s Norte, The End Of History. Despite 35 entries since 1953, the country has yet to secure a nomination in the category. International sales: Luxbox

Singapore: Stranger Eyes (Yeo Siew Hua)
Yeo’s fourth feature is a thriller about a man obsessively searching for his missing daughter after receiving disturbing videos that expose his secrets. Wu Chien-Ho, Lee Kang-Sheng and Anicca Panna lead the cast. The film debuted in Competition at Venice Film Festival in 2024, going on to play New York, Hamburg, BFI London Film Festival and opening the Singapore Film Festival. Lee won best supporting actor at the 2025 Asian Film Awards for his role. Singapore entered the international feature award for the 1960 ceremony, but didn’t enter another title until Eric Khoo’s Be With Me in 2005. It has no nominations from 18 previous entries to date, including Yeo’s own A Land Imagined for the 2020 awards. International sales: Playtime

South Korea: No Other Choice (Park Chan-wook)
Read the full story here.

Taiwan: Left-Handed Girl (Shih-Ching Tsou)
Tsou’s solo directing debut is produced, edited and co-written by Sean Baker, the US director of Oscar-winner Anora. The Taipei-set drama follows a single mother and her two daughters who move from the countryside to open a food stall at a bustling night market. The film premiered in Cannes’ Critics’ Week. Mike Goodridge from Good Chaos is also a producer on the Taiwan-France-US-UK co-production, which was acquired by Netflix for most of the world. Taiwanese-American filmmaker Tsou co-directed 2004’s Take Out with Baker, and produced his features Tangerine, The Florida Project and Red Rocket. Taiwan last made the shortlist in 2020 with Chung Mong-Hong’s family drama A Sun. Prior to that, the previous shortlisted entry was Wei Te-sheng’s Warriors Of The Rainbow: Seediq Bale in 2012. The last to achieve a nomination was Ang Lee’s martial-arts epic Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, which went on to win the award and three further Oscars in 2001. International sales: Le Pacte

Tajikistan: Black Rabbit, White Rabbit (Shahram Mokri)
The Iranian filmmaker explores fear and fragility in a story of three people’s intertwined destinies. The film first premiered at Busan where it won the Vision Asia award and will play in competition at the BFI London Film Festival later this month. It is produced by Karnameh Dubai Company. International sales: DreamLab Films

Thailand: A Useful Ghost (Ratchapoom Boonbunchachoke)
This supernatural drama won the Grand Prix in the Critics’ Week sidebar at Cannes after becoming the first Thai film selected on the Croisette in 10 years. Local superstar Davika Hoorne from box-­office hit Pee Mak plays a dead woman who returns to her husband by possessing a vacuum cleaner and offers to be a useful ghost and get rid of useless spirits. The debut feature is produced by Cattleya Paosrijaroen and Soros Sukhum of Thailand’s 185 Films, alongside France’s Haut Les Mains, Singapore’s Momo Film and Germany’s Mayana Film. It marks the country’s 32nd submission to the Oscars with no nominations to date. However, it did make the shortlist last year with Pat Boonnitipat’s How To Make Millions Before Grandma Dies. International sales: Best Friend Forever

Vietnam: Red Rain (Dang Thai Huyen)
Tells the story of the 81-day defence of the Quảng Trị Citadel in 1972, a key battle in the Vietnam War. The highest-grossing Vietnamese film of all time after grossing $28m. The country has been nominated once, in 1993 for The Scent of Green Papaya. International sales: TBC
